observations: === (a) GATING / TEACHER-TARGET IDEAS (mapped to RUNBOOK-4 knobs) ===  AM paper (2602.16284) faithful TEACHER/TARGET + VALUE-SOLVE we must not drift from: teacher = the ORIGINAL attention OUTPUT Attn(q;K,V) AND the ORIGINAL attention MASS Mass(q;K)=sum_j exp(qK_j^T/sqrt d), matched over a set of reference queries Q_ref (two objectives: Eq1 output-match, Eq2 mass-match). VALUE SOLVE is closed-form ordinary least squares C_v*=(X^T X)^-1 X^T Y with X = compacted softmax features exp(qC_k^T+beta)/Z and Y = teacher outputs (torch.linalg.lstsq, FP32 then BF16). IMPORTANT: the paper tested L2 ridge on the (beta,C_v) solve and found it DEGRADED performance for ALL lambda>0 -> keep RIDGE on the value solve ~0 (our RIDGE_LAMBDA default 1e-4 already tiny; note RUNBOOK-7's lambda=2.0 sweet spot is a DIFFERENT solve, the Phase-1 recon, not the value solve). beta is fit by NNLS to match mass (w_j=exp(beta_j)>=0, m_i approx sum_j w_j exp(q_i C_k_j^T)); stability clamps beta in [-3,3] for highest-attn keys, beta>=-7 prune for OMP. AM's explicit STANCE on our core 'low-attention-mass slot selection' problem: AM does NOT update or select low-mass slots; it (i) SELECTS high-mass keys as the write support (highest-attention keys via RMS-aggregated attention weight, OR OMP greedy mass-residual matching, Alg 1/2), and (ii) CORRECTS the mass deficit that subsetting creates with the per-token beta bias. The paper argues drop/merge WITHOUT biases SYSTEMATICALLY UNDERESTIMATES the compacted block's future attention contribution -> the AM-faithful cure for 'low mass' is to let beta reweight retained high-mass slots to carry the missing mass, not to gate into low-mass slots. Knob map: highest-attn keys -> SLOT_SELECTION=attention_mass / KEY_MODE=highest_attention; OMP -> KEY_MODE=omp; mass-matching bias -> ENABLE_BETA=1, BETA_FIT_SCOPE; support budget -> TOP_T; nonuniform per-head budgets (AM finds head sensitivity input-invariant, precomputed greedy budget = MOST important ablation) -> GRANULARITY=per_head + a per-head TOP_T schedule (MIN_TOP_T_PER_LAYER). Ref-query source: self-study best, context-prefill/repeat-prefill ~as good and much faster, random-vectors lags; on-policy (compact layers sequentially, re-extract queries) small consistent gain -> QUERIES_PER_BATCH. TF-IDF paper (2510.15103) 'which slots': pick top-t slots by TF-IDF = HIGH access on the NEW batch (TF) but LOW access on a BACKGROUND corpus (IDF, the corpus to PRESERVE) -> SLOT_SELECTION=tfidf, USE_IDF=1, BG_STATS_PATH, IDF_SMOOTHING, IDF_TOP_K. Findings: TF-IDF beats TF-only ESPECIALLY at small t; the gap shrinks as t->all-slots (IDF matters less when you update everything). Background-corpus choice matters: ranking vs the LEARNING set weakens retention; vs held-out/pretraining preserves it -> our background MUST be Phase-1 QA (confirms d). Optimizer: SGD >> AdamW for sparse memory finetuning (Adam's adaptive step/momentum interacts badly with sparsity, more forgetting) -> for any sparse-GRADIENT point prefer SGD (wandb confirms: SGD value-only keeps QA 1.69 but barely learns MT 3.22; adam value-only forgets QA to 2.54 but learns MT to 1.76). TF-IDF's stance on low-mass: raw access MAGNITUDE is the wrong signal; SPECIFICITY (TF/IDF) is right -- a slot with low overall attention but high new-doc-specific access is exactly the one to write; do NOT overwrite generically-useful (high-background) slots. Synthesis of the two: AM cares about MASS PRESERVATION (read side: freeze keys + beta), TF-IDF cares about ACCESS SPECIFICITY (write side: which value-slots). CANDIDATE single-variable hypotheses (orchestrator decides, not me): H-a1 SLOT_SELECTION=attention_mass vs tfidf; H-a2 ENABLE_BETA=1 vs unset under attention_mass (test AM mass-bias); H-a3 KEY_MODE=omp vs freeze (RISKY -- RUNBOOK-7 says key updates collapse QA to ~16-19 floor, so OMP as a WRITE-key selector may only be safe as read-side support); H-a4 IDF_PRIOR_WEIGHT>0 to blend IDF into attention_mass (hybrid gater); H-a5 at TOP_T=32, USE_IDF=1 vs 0 (test 'IDF matters more at small t').  === (b) CARTRIDGE COST FIGURES (T3 story) ===  Cartridges paper (2506.06266): 38.6x less memory, 26.4x higher throughput vs ICL; TRAINING a Cartridge on an 8B model ~30 min on an 8xH100 node per corpus = ~4 H100-GPU-hours/corpus (Stanford HAI / HazyResearch blog; the 8.5MB PDF would not text-extract via WebFetch, so figure is from the authors' summaries -- treat as authoritative-secondary). AM paper Table 5 (replicates Cartridges training compute, ~same self-study tokens/context-token as original): QuALITY (7k ctx) ~5 H100-hours + 25-30M self-study tokens/article (32,768 self-study samples, 1 epoch, LR 2e-2); LongHealth-5 (60k) ~15 H100-hrs + 100-150M tokens; LongHealth-10 (120k) 300M tokens. AM Table 3 (self-study query-gen proxy, 60k LongHealth Gemma-3-12B, 1xH200): self-study 139s vs repeat-prefill 8s vs context-prefill 7s per context. So the two cartridge cost terms AM aims to kill are, on OUR box: synthesis ~10-12 ks/task + gradient Phase-2 ~1.8 ks; AM's closed-form T1/T2 (seconds-to-minutes) is the contrast.
